entries.summary: Most Gemini prototypes start the same way. You grab an API key from Google AI Studio, then paste it into your coding agent to start building a prototype.
entries.text: Most Gemini prototypes start the same way. You grab an API key from Google AI Studio, then paste it into your coding agent to start building a prototype. That speed is the point, and shouldn’t be slowed down. The trouble starts later, when the prototype gets real users and the key comes along unchanged. By then it usually isn't one key. Every developer has their own, often several, sitting in .env files, shell profiles and chat threads. The app has one more, baked into its config. For example, imagine an account that normally spends $180 a month. One of those keys ends up in a public repo, a Slack channel or a mobile app bundle. Automated scrapers find it within minutes and use it to run large workloads. By the time the first billing alert arrives, the bill is in the tens of thousands. Under the shared responsibility model, the customer pays for usage made with their own valid credentials. For a seed-stage company, that’s runway gone in a weekend. In our recent post, 10 questions every startup should answer before moving to production with their AI prototype, we covered the whole path from prototype to production. This post goes deeper on one part of it: getting off raw API keys entirely. Here is what this guide covers: Authorize your people. Give everyone on the team one login with Application Default Credentials and use it to call Gemini, Claude and open models. Steps 1 and 2 take about five minutes. Authorize your application. entries.summary: When an Airflow pipeline fails in production, the hard part is rarely the fix. It's finding out what to fix. A task dies without a traceback.
entries.text: When an Airflow pipeline fails in production, the hard part is rarely the fix. It's finding out what to fix. A task dies without a traceback. Is it the code, the data, or the environment? Hard to say, as clues are scattered across task logs, scheduler logs, and worker metrics. And once you know what the problem is, the question becomes whether to add memory, rewrite the DAG, or finally take on the major version upgrade you've been putting off. Answering these questions takes time and deep Airflow expertise, usually while you're on call in the middle of an incident. AI agents can increasingly do much of this legwork. Managed Service for Apache Airflow (formerly Cloud Composer) now offers agentic help across a pipeline's entire lifecycle. In the Google Cloud console, Managed Airflow Agent investigates failed tasks, recommends improvements to your environment, and checks whether your DAGs are ready for a newer Airflow version. In your IDE or coding agent, Data Agent Kit writes, migrates, and deploys DAGs. In this post, we take you on a tour of these features through a story of a fictional company, Cymbal Shops. Meet Cymbal Shops, where every click counts Amira is a data engineer at Cymbal Shops, an online retailer running cymbal-prod, a production Managed Airflow (Gen 3) environment whose workers have 2 vCPUs, 4 GB of memory, and that autoscale between 1 and 6. entries.title: Drowning in clicks: Scaling Black Friday pipelines with Managed Airflow agents

entries.summary: Imagine you're building a data agent to answer questions about an enterprise data warehouse.
entries.text: Imagine you're building a data agent to answer questions about an enterprise data warehouse. Ideally, you'd develop and test it against production data, but access restrictions and data sensitivity make that difficult – especially when the engineers building the agent sit outside the team that owns the data. Even with access, a live warehouse is a poor test track: Catalog descriptions are often incomplete or contradicted by institutional knowledge in docs and chat threads; there’s no verified answer key across its thousands of tables; and you can't systematically vary the complexity of the data and documents to see where the agent breaks. So teams often test on toy datasets and hope the agent holds up in production. Other disciplines test differently. Automobile designers study aerodynamics by putting a scale model in a wind tunnel, which reproduces the airflow forces that matter while ignoring surface details like paint and badges. A shape that performs well in the tunnel performs well on the road because the tunnel preserves the physical properties the shape responds to. Data agents need a wind tunnel too: a synthetic data estate (the databases, documents, and chat history where a company's knowledge lives) with the same structure and causal behavior as a real organization, while synthesizing every name, number, and document. It is designed to preserve what the agent reasons over: how tables relate, what business events create which records, where institutional knowledge li
entries.title: Frontier and Center: Why your data agents need a “wind tunnel”

entries.text: In global maritime logistics, Marine Ports and Terminals play a significant role in the movement of container and cargo, within and beyond. Marine ports and terminals world-wide use a Terminal Operating System (TOS) which acts as the central nervous system managing port operations 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. A modern TOS plans, automates and orchestrates every physical and digital activities, resources and events across Order-to-Invoice processes of a marine terminal. Developed by Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), DynaPORT is a field-proven next-generation Terminal Operating System that provides a single, integrated operating backbone for multimodal and multipurpose terminals. It orchestrates the complete order-to-invoice lifecycle across vessel, rail, truck, and barge operations, while supporting containers, general cargo, dry and liquid bulk, break-bulk, and roll-on/roll-off cargo. By automating end-to-end terminal workflows, DynaPORT delivers real-time operational visibility into operations while optimizing assets and resources to drive improvement of key business performance indicators. One of India’s largest commercial port developers and operators has relied on DynaPORT for more than two decades across its cargo terminals, supporting the management of bulk, break-bulk, and liquid cargo. Over the past year, customer use of Managed Service for Apache Spark in serverless deployments has nearly doubled, with millions of jobs running each month as enterprises build on Google’s Agentic Data Cloud. In the Agentic Data Cloud, Apache Spark doesn't operate in isolation. Managed Service for Apache Spark runs on Google Cloud's borderless lakehouse, so Apache Spark and BigQuery can read and write the same tables with high performance. Through Knowledge Catalog, both engines share centralized governance, consistent policies, detailed lineage, and semantic discovery for AI agents. Today, we are announcing the general availability of Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, debuting a next-generation runtime foundation for serverless and managed cluster deployments. Engineered to power both modern enterprise data pipelines and fast-growing agentic workloads, Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 introduces: A new 4.0 runtime with Apache Spark 4.2: Standardized on Apach

entries.summary: Ever wonder how the Google Ads team keeps the massive system stable and online, despite continuous attempts by hackers to take it down?
entries.text: Ever wonder how the Google Ads team keeps the massive system stable and online, despite continuous attempts by hackers to take it down? Part of the answer is using Spanner as its core operational and graph database. The Google Ads team uses a central graph-based platform to fight fraud and abuse with batch and real-time signals. Built to protect the Google Ads ecosystem and now used by multiple teams across Google, the platform organizes anti-abuse intelligence into a single, interconnected view. Its core mission is simple but critical: uncover hidden connections between malicious assets in real time before they can harm users or advertisers. This blog talks about the challenging modern fraud and abuse landscape, and how Spanner, specifically Spanner Graph, helps Google successfully detect those threats. The rising cost and sophistication of modern fraud The need for a graph-based abuse detection platform stems from how the global threat landscape has evolved. Digital advertising fraud and online scams are no longer minor operational nuisances, they are a massive drain on the global economy. According to the NASDAQ Global Financial Crime Report, total global fraud losses are estimated at nearly $580 billion for 2025. Furthermore, global surveys indicate that approximately one in five adults fall victim to scams. In digital ads, fraud and abuse waste marketing spend, corrupt attribution data, and expose everyday users to financial scams, identity theft, and malware. Bad actors

entries.text: Network sidecars have a deserved reputation for excessive resource consumption and increased management overhead, especially in a service mesh environment. Today, we are announcing the general availability of ambient networking for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). This milestone marks an important evolution in how your run service mesh on GKE, bringing a sidecar-less architecture into production. Introduced earlier this year, ambient networking decouples functionality traditionally provided as a service mesh from application workloads, allowing platform operators and developers to help secure, observe, and route traffic without the resource overhead and operational complexity of managing sidecar proxies. Ambient networking architecture The ambient networking architecture shifts networking responsibilities from individual application pods to shared per-node components and managed control plane services. Certificate Authority Service: Authenticate workloads and dynamically issues managed workload identity certificates, on-demand to enable seamless mTLS encryption across service-to-service communication. entries.summary: As organizations scale their cloud footprint to thousands of autonomous agents and microservices, you can accidentally create an operational bottleneck with strict Identity and Access Management (IAM).
entries.text: As organizations scale their cloud footprint to thousands of autonomous agents and microservices, you can accidentally create an operational bottleneck with strict Identity and Access Management (IAM). Meanwhile, administrators still need to enforce least privilege across thousands of resources without slowing down engineering velocity. Enter Unified Access Policies (UAPs), Google Cloud's next-generation access control engine in Cloud IAM, now in preview at no additional cost. UAP consolidates allow and deny rules into one unified schema, and decouples policy definition from resource enforcement. This approach allows you to author a policy once and bind it across your organization. UAP governs human, workload, and first-class agent identities with your existing IAM policies. With UAP, you can radically simplify your access policies and manage them more easily at scale. Scale limitations of legacy access models Traditional access policy models can push teams into a tough trade-off between Zero Trust access and pipeline speed due to three compounding forces: Fragmented schemas and permission sprawl: In granting thousands of granular permissions across cloud resources, administrators are forced to choose between either over-granting permissions from coarse roles with broad access, or wrangling two different syntaxes (APIs and mental models across allow and deny) just to define one workload's custom access posture. entries.summary: Welcome to The Blueprint, our ongoing series where we highlight how Google Cloud customers are tackling unique and common challenges across industries using the latest AI and cloud technologies.
entries.text: Welcome to The Blueprint, our ongoing series where we highlight how Google Cloud customers are tackling unique and common challenges across industries using the latest AI and cloud technologies. We hope to inspire others looking to innovate in their work. Kult is a London-based startup building a companion experience for games. It sits alongside your session, understands the game you are playing and where you are in it, and answers by voice and on a second screen. The more you play with it, the better it knows how you like to play. The challenge Traditionally, getting help in the middle of a game meant alt-tabbing, opening a video, scrolling a forum, and hoping you find the answer before you forget why you looked. Information should come to the player instead. As gamers ourselves, our team wanted a way for someone to be able to ask a question out loud, hands on the keyboard or controller, hear an answer, and consult a second screen if needed, without interrupting their immersion in the game. Three things decide whether that works: latency, accuracy and cost. Latency: Games are time-sensitive. The answer has to be fast, and the interaction should feel like asking a friend who’s an expert on the game, sitting on the couch next to you and watching you play. Accuracy: General-purpose models have training cutoffs. They can be months out of date and are often wrong about a specific game, patch, or build — and a wrong answer can be costly in the game and a waste of the player's time
entries.title: The Blueprint: How Kult built a gaming companion that actually knows your game

entries.text: GKE Dataplane V2 is Google Cloud’s next-generation networking dataplane for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and open-source Cilium to replace traditional iptables routing and kube-proxy. We built GKE Dataplane V2 to meet the performance, scalability, and security demands of modern cloud-native workloads. GKE customers consistently tell us that while they want to adopt GKE Dataplane V2 for its performance and scale, migrating production clusters carrying stateful workloads and established IP allocations has been challenging, often requiring a disruptive parallel cluster setup. Today, we are pleased to introduce the preview of in-place migration, allowing you to transition eligible VPC-native clusters from GKE Dataplane V1 to GKE Dataplane V2 directly. Let’s take a look at what GKE Dataplane V2 brings to the table and how to start migrating your environment to it. Why GKE Dataplane V2? GKE Dataplane V2 is built on the extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and open-source Cilium, with features specifically tuned for performance, scalability, and deep integration with Google Cloud networking. Consider the following capabilities: Scale and performance: By handling packet processing with eBPF maps in the Linux kernel instead of linear iptables rules, GKE Dataplane V2 supports clusters of up to 15,000 nodes with network policy enforcement (and up to 65,000 nodes when network policy enforcement is disabled, which requires recreating cl
entries.title: Introducing in-place migration to GKE Dataplane V2

We also described some of the threat actor’s post-exploitation operations. In this blog we describe additional post-compromise activity involving the exploitation of a vulnerability in VMware vCenter and the deployment of additional malware families. The vCenter server is a centralized platform deployed as a Photon Linux virtual appliance and is used to configure, control, and monitor ESXi host environments. CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC). Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local. entries.summary: In June we introduced the Open Knowledge Format (OKF), an open specification that provides plain markdown and YAML to give agents the context they need.
entries.text: In June we introduced the Open Knowledge Format (OKF), an open specification that provides plain markdown and YAML to give agents the context they need. In July, v0.2 added trust signals: provenance, trust, freshness, lifecycle, and attestation. In production, bundles move between organizations, multiple agents edit the same corpus, and independent tools need to read a bundle the same way. Released today, OKF v0.3 adds precise conformance rules, trust tiers that keep pace with agent edits, self-describing bundles with licensing, safe ways to retire and move knowledge, a stable extension model, and a clear versioning policy. However, the core idea behind OKF stays the same: type is still the only required field, and your existing bundles keep working. We're also launching OKF use cases, which are community guides for using OKF alongside other industry standards, and two agent skills that let coding agents write and read OKF bundles. Finally, to make cross-organization collaboration easier, we’re moving OKF out of the Google Cloud Platform GitHub org into a standalone organization at https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/. Let’s take a closer look at what’s new in OKF v0.3. Built for interoperability v0.3 adds a formal conformance section, allowing independent producers and consumers to work together by design. The spec is self-contained and uses RFC 2119 keywords. It gives one clear answer to the questions that come up when tools from different teams a
entries.title: What’s new in OKF v0.3: enterprise-ready knowledge, use cases, and skills

entries.summary: Applying recommendations to a production database can feel risky if you can’t easily quantify the performance benefit or justify the additional cost.
entries.text: Applying recommendations to a production database can feel risky if you can’t easily quantify the performance benefit or justify the additional cost. While Database Center flags fleet-level health issues and provides proactive recommendations, database administrators still face the challenge of testing recommended changes without disrupting live applications or spending hours manually configuring staging replicas. To help solve this problem, we’re excited to announce the preview of assessments in Database Center for Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. Assessments is an agentic workflow that lets you run automated, isolated synthetic benchmarks on cloned instances, helping you verify potential performance gains before touching your production environment. Moving from recommendations to production changes Managing production databases means balancing system stability, performance, and infrastructure spend. When Database Center alerts you to a potential bottleneck and recommends a change, you need to evaluate the change before you can implement it. That workflow can be complex: Setting up dedicated staging environments to mirror production settings Running benchmark workloads to simulate real-world traffic Measuring latency, throughput, and resource saturation before and after applying changes Calculating whether performance gains justify potential cost adjustments Because this manual benchmarking process takes a lot of time and engineering effort, it’s easy to put off making critical upd
